title: How does the internet actually move data?
seoTitle: How the Internet Moves Data: DNS, Routers and Packets Explained
seoDescription: Follow a web request through DNS, IP packets, routers, fiber networks, CDNs and servers to understand how internet data actually travels.
excerpt: A page can cross networks and continents in milliseconds. Here is what happens between typing a URL and receiving the response.
author: KitsuWire Editorial
keyTakeaways: Internet data is divided into packets that routers forward between interconnected networks.
DNS translates human-readable domain names into addresses used to reach services.
TCP or QUIC and TLS provide transport and secure communication for modern web traffic.
CDNs reduce latency by serving content from locations closer to users.
body: When you open a website, the page rarely travels to you as one object from one machine. Your device resolves a name, establishes secure communication and exchanges packets across several networks.
The internet works because independently operated networks agree on common protocols and exchange reachability information.

sections.heading: Step 1: DNS finds where to connect
paragraphs: Humans use names such as kitsuwire.com, while network communication ultimately needs an IP address. DNS resolvers look up records for the requested hostname, often using cached results to avoid repeating the full lookup.
Large services may return different addresses depending on geography, load balancing or CDN design.

sections.heading: Step 2: your device creates packets
paragraphs: Application data is carried by transport protocols and then encapsulated into IP packets. Packets contain addressing information that lets network devices forward them toward their destination.
Web traffic commonly uses TCP with TLS or HTTP/3 over QUIC. These protocols solve different problems including reliable delivery, congestion control and encrypted communication.

sections.heading: Step 3: routers choose paths
paragraphs: Your home or mobile network forwards traffic to an internet service provider. Routers then move packets through networks based on routing tables rather than following one globally fixed path.
Between large networks, the Border Gateway Protocol helps autonomous systems advertise which IP prefixes they can reach. Commercial agreements and routing policies influence the resulting paths.

sections.heading: Step 4: fiber carries the bits
paragraphs: Most long-distance internet capacity travels as light through fiber-optic cables. Submarine cables connect continents, while terrestrial fiber connects cities, data centers and exchange points.
Satellites and wireless links are important in specific access scenarios, but the global internet backbone is heavily dependent on fiber infrastructure.

sections.heading: Step 5: CDNs bring content closer
paragraphs: Content delivery networks place cached content at many edge locations. A user in Europe may therefore receive images or scripts from a nearby CDN site rather than from the website's origin server on another continent.
Reducing physical distance and network hops can improve latency and also reduce load on origin infrastructure.

sections.heading: What happens when a packet is lost?
paragraphs: Networks are not perfect. Congestion, faulty links and wireless conditions can cause packet loss. Reliable transports detect missing data and retransmit when necessary, while congestion-control algorithms adjust sending behavior.
The remarkable part of the internet is not that failures never occur. It is that protocols and redundant paths are designed to continue operating despite many local failures.

faq.question: Does internet traffic always take the shortest physical route?
faq.answer: No. Routing depends on network topology, policy, peering and available paths, so the chosen route may not be geographically shortest.

faq.question: What does DNS do?
faq.answer: DNS maps domain names to records such as IP addresses so clients can locate services.

faq.question: Why does distance affect latency?
faq.answer: Signals cannot travel instantly. Propagation through fiber plus routing, processing and queueing add delay, so longer paths generally increase latency.
